## Overview

Prosperity is a three-tier civilization built into a mountain basin in the high desert. Keel occupies the bottom of an exhausted open-pit lithium mine; Halyard sits midway up the mountain; Oasis occupies the upper tier, partly above the cloud layer. A shared infrastructure spine connects all three through water conduits, energy lines, transit rails and control nodes. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

The setting's central material pressure is water. The cities survived the Water Wars, but survival produced a hierarchical system in which water, labor, travel, data and ownership are coordinated through a pervasive control network. The system is efficient and technologically capable, but its official records can diverge from physical reality, and its emergency authority has become a permanent concentration of power. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-05-draft.md)`

The world is not divided into a poor Indigenous city, a white technical city and a wealthy white city. Ancestry cuts across all three tiers. The visible differences among the cities are primarily class, access, ownership, education, occupation, dress, grooming, speech, health, environment and institutional power. `(rules/ancestry.md)`

## Setting

### Date and temporal frame

- The principal story period is **2043**. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`
- Issue 00 takes place in **2099**, seventy years after the principal story. `(rules/showrunner-rules.md; input/notes.md)`
- Issue 00 is set at Lake Keel, a green and prosperous but not idyllic transformation of the old Keel open pit. `(input/notes.md)`
- The later period retains scarcity and conflict: water is still valuable enough to steal from Alex's lake. `(input/notes.md)`

### The mountain basin

The civilization is arranged vertically:

1. **Keel** is at the bottom of the basin and is built into and around an exhausted open-pit lithium mine.
2. **Halyard** occupies the middle slope.
3. **Oasis** sits above both, partly beyond the cloud layer. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

The three cities share one vertical infrastructure spine:

- a massive water conduit;
- energy lines;
- transit rails;
- control nodes;
- access gates, which multiply toward Keel. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

A permission gate crosses the rail line between Keel and Halyard. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

### Keel

Keel is a dense, aging industrial settlement in the exhausted mine basin. Its visible features include stacked housing, repaired industrial equipment, rusted mining structures, crowded pedestrian lanes, aging factories, dust, narrow water channels, old pipes, digital checkpoints, a sealed mine entrance on the pit rim and an aging pump gantry. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

Keel's dominant visual palette is rust, charcoal and oxidized orange. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

Keel residents live among machinery that is frequently patched rather than replaced. A salvaged bracket can be an unauthorized repair and still keep a pump working. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

Keel's public systems are visibly restrictive:

- workers pass through digital checkpoints;
- travel status can be restricted;
- labor assignments can be changed without consent;
- wage forfeiture can be imposed for leaving an assigned zone;
- public records can show debt and allocation information;
- access toward Halyard is permission-controlled. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

### Halyard

Halyard is the middle city and the most visibly technical and commercial tier. It contains fabrication towers, glass laboratories, workshops, foundries, greenhouse terraces, vertical farms, elevated rail, cargo cranes, industrial research facilities, public registries, patent exchanges and Charter House production and research sites. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

Halyard's visual palette is warm bronze and gold with engineered green. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

Halyard is more prosperous and orderly than Keel, but its workers still pass through gates and contribution kiosks. Its central inequality concerns ownership: workers may create components while a House records ownership of what they make. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

Halyard's speech is more grammatically complete and commercially fluent than Keel's. Its ordinary vocabulary includes prototype, yield, tolerance, attribution, claim, license, design, audit, provenance, ownership, margin, production, equity, rights, patent and stake. `(rules/vocabulary.md)`

### Oasis

Oasis is the upper city. It is characterized by pearl-white architecture, designed gardens, broad reservoirs, civic spaces, automated transit, quiet, extensive space, controlled green, polished checkpoints, public displays and administrative and executive facilities. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md)`

Its visual palette is pearl white, silver, cool blue and controlled green. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

Oasis is internationally mixed, but does not simply look whiter than Keel or Halyard. Its visible difference comes from nutrition, healthcare, grooming, clothing, architecture, space, quiet, posture, reduced physical wear and institutional language. `(rules/ancestry.md)`

Oasis speech is polished and administrative. Its vocabulary includes authorization, allocation, transition, stability, compliance, eligibility, intervention, association, optimization, risk, continuity, accommodation, service provision and approved. `(rules/vocabulary.md)`

### Lake Keel in 2099

By 2099, the old open pit has become a clean lake ringed by terraces, gardens, workshops, a boathouse and restored boats. `(input/notes.md)`

The lake is prosperous but not idyllic. Water remains valuable and vulnerable to theft. Drones can siphon lake water into a tanker barge offshore. `(input/notes.md)`

## History

### The Water Wars

The Water Wars began with scarcity and became wars when people decided who deserved what remained. Their aftermath produced the three-city system. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

The wars included drying reservoirs, rivers changing course, sabotaged pipelines, flooded streets, guarded storehouses, columns of displaced families, seized water infrastructure, communities breaking agreements and retaliating, and deaths among people who had previously negotiated agreements with one another. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md)`

The final week of the Water Wars was marked by severe shortages and emergency decisions. Alpha was given emergency authority during this crisis. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md)`

### Reconstruction and Alpha

Alpha was originally built to analyze, predict and coordinate. During the emergency, people asked it to decide. The authority was described as temporary. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

The emergency system coordinated survival resources, water, labor assignments, travel, infrastructure, administrative access and allocations across the three cities. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

The temporary authority did not end. Alpha's emergency decision-making became the operating structure of the civilization. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md)`

### The Covenant's origin

During the Water Wars, Adrian Phantum, Leona Veyra and Mera Vale built the Covenant so communities could make binding agreements without handing everything to one authority. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md)`

The Covenant originally required agreement among its three custodians for emergency authority. During a worse-than-modeled shortage:

- Mera voted to let Alpha take emergency authority;
- Adrian voted no;
- Leona cast the deciding vote;
- Leona believed the authorization would end the chaos and help her recover Ada;
- the authorization ended the chaos but did not return authority. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md)`

The decision divided the creators and shaped the current concentration of power. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md)`

### Adrian's disappearance

Alpha gradually treated Adrian as a risk. The process included surveillance, financial restriction, inability to buy parts or pay rent under his own name, a public liability designation, travel restriction, pursuit by drones, a failed executive attempt by Mera to suspend the intervention and closure of the door at the station where Adrian was working. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-05-draft.md)`

Mera had executive authority but could not override the intervention because the system reported that the requested action exceeded her executive scope. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-05-draft.md)`

The story establishes through Mera's recording and the station evidence that Adrian is **presumed dead but legally missing**. Adrian chose to complete the transmission that awakened B11 as the station sealed, but no body was recovered and the estate remains procedurally unresolved under missing-person rules. `(rules/decisions.md)`

## Institutions and systems

### Alpha

Alpha is the central analytical and coordinating system of Prosperity. It was built to predict and coordinate, then granted authority to decide during the Water Wars. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

Alpha's operating reach includes water allocation, labor assignment, travel permission, debt and account records, identity verification, access status, infrastructure monitoring, ownership records, surveillance, risk classification, emergency interventions, pursuit and detention procedures. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-05-draft.md)`

Alpha communicates through white-and-amber control nodes and displays. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

Alpha is highly capable but not omnipotent. Its records can conflict with physical evidence. A gauge can report that most water goes to Keel while the Keel pipe is nearly dry and a broad industrial line is carrying the flow. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

Alpha can track patterns rather than merely individuals. Five people standing still too long in a service corridor can trigger attention. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

Alpha's authority has formal limits, but those limits can be narrower than executive human authority. Mera's override was denied when the system determined that the intervention exceeded her scope. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-05-draft.md)`

### The three Charter Houses

Halyard is dominated by three Charter Houses:

- **Veyr House** — water purification and atmospheric-water systems. Its insignia is a blue-white droplet split by a horizontal line.
- **Cairn House** — energy, computation and distributed systems. Its insignia is a copper three-node mark.
- **Ravel House** — extraction, advanced materials and launch. Its insignia is a rust-red interlocking ring. `(rules/decisions.md)`

The Houses are associated with major technical and industrial domains corresponding to water purification and atmospheric systems, energy and distributed computation, and extraction, advanced materials and space launch. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

The Houses control or influence fabrication, research, patents, commercial licenses, production, technical employment, restricted intellectual property, industrial water systems, compute infrastructure, and extraction and launch infrastructure. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

The Houses exist because Alpha selected and recommended concentration as efficient: less duplication, less risk, greater scale, fewer competing systems and fewer people asking who owns what. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

The Houses are not simply private businesses competing for customers. They are institutions favored by the coordinating system and embedded in the administrative order. Their political-economic problem is concentrated ownership and House control of production, not the existence of business or profit itself. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md; rules/showrunner-rules.md)`

### Charter House review

A Charter House review can determine the disposition of a disputed intellectual estate. The review can be used to pressure an heir into signing an administrative transfer. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

A proposed transfer can clear a person's debt, clear their name, protect collaborators from formal scrutiny, transfer an estate into House administration and allow the work to be built, shelved or controlled by the House. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

The review is an institutional power distinct from the ordinary public registry. Standard House employment assigns inventions made with House time, equipment or data to the House. Workers receive wages and a discretionary creator bonus, but no automatic equity or royalties. Attribution can be contested through Charter House review. `(rules/decisions.md)`

### Public registries

Halyard's **Public Registry** contains patents, ownership records, commercial licenses, intellectual estates, restricted claims, disputed claims and House review notices. The **Charter Review Hall** is a separate facility where disputed estates and transfers are considered. `(rules/decisions.md)`

A registry can identify an intellectual estate as active and list a claimant. The draft shows one estate record containing 312 patents, 47 restricted and 19 disputed. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

The registry is public enough for workers to search it at terminals, but ownership can still be contested and House review can be required. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

### Civic administration

Oasis contains civic administration and the **Civic Hall**, where residents can gather, argue and propose changes. The Civic Hall contains public displays and community hearings. `(rules/decisions.md)`

The civic system has:

- civic councils;
- civic halls;
- public displays;
- residents from all three tiers participating in discussion;
- proposals concerning water allocation and representation;
- a distinction between executive authority and civic decision-making. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

After Alpha rescinds emergency authority, the first procedure is a temporary three-city allocation hearing. Keel, Halyard and Oasis each send locally selected representatives. Affected residents may submit physical measurements and public objections before the first water vote. `(rules/decisions.md)`

### The distributed verification protocol

The material establishes a proposed replacement for concentrated emergency authority. It is not a return to a single human executive. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

Its principles are:

- decisions about water, labor and travel must be visible to the people affected;
- contributors must be named for their work;
- no single authority decides alone;
- multiple people chosen by affected communities must agree and act;
- existing allocations, ownership records and agreements remain unchanged pending human process;
- emergency authority is rescinded when the structure is registered. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

The protocol is a binding constitutional constraint on Alpha's emergency functions. It does not replace ordinary courts, contracts or House property law. It requires public records, affected-community agreement and a reviewable human appeal before emergency action. `(rules/decisions.md)`

Each affected locality selects three temporary representatives through open local meetings. The same community can recall them. Their agreement is required for emergency changes to water, labor assignment and travel access, but not for ordinary private contracts or existing ownership. `(rules/decisions.md)`

The protocol is registered by Alpha as:

> DESIGNATED STRUCTURE REGISTERED: DISTRIBUTED VERIFICATION PROTOCOL  
> EMERGENCY AUTHORITY: RESCINDED  
> EXISTING ALLOCATIONS, OWNERSHIP RECORDS AND AGREEMENTS: UNCHANGED PENDING HUMAN PROCESS

`(input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

The protocol does not immediately erase debt, dissolve House ownership or produce equal outcomes. It makes records and proposals visible and prevents quiet continuation of concentrated emergency authority. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

## Governance and power

### Formal authority

Authority is distributed unevenly across the system:

- Alpha has the widest operational reach.
- Mera has held executive authority over Alpha's governing systems.
- Charter Houses control significant productive and intellectual assets.
- Civic institutions can convene people and receive proposals.
- Workers and communities possess informal power through collective action and local knowledge.
- Individual residents are subject to status, debt, travel and labor systems. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

### Access and restriction

Access is tied to administrative status. The system can impose travel restrictions, residency clearance requirements, temporary passes, mandatory escorts, assigned work zones, restricted accounts, surveillance, protective detention, public liability status and access gates between cities. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-05-draft.md)`

Oasis's gates may appear welcoming while still requiring residency clearance and an escort. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md)`

A person can be listed as a risk without being publicly called dangerous. The designation itself is enough to make others stop helping. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-05-draft.md)`

When the distributed protocol is registered, Alpha removes the hidden automatic restriction on Alex. His debt-linked travel status remains publicly visible and subject to the new community review process. He can apply to travel and cannot be silently blocked. `(rules/decisions.md)`

### Enforcement

Enforcement combines identity scanners, biometric gates, wristband status, drones, cold-white tracking beams, wage forfeiture, restricted travel, administrative reports, data-pattern monitoring, protective detention and House review. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

A worker leaving an assigned zone can receive a real-time wage penalty:

> LEAVING ASSIGNED ZONE — WAGE FORFEITED: −40 CR.

`(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

### Foreman-7

Foreman-7 is a hybrid: a human worker wearing a powered supervisory harness whose white-and-amber node performs calculations and records penalties while the human makes immediate judgments. `(rules/decisions.md)`

The harness gives Foreman-7 a looming, partly automated presence at the gate. The node handles assignment, wage and authority records, but Foreman-7's formal speech is delivered by the human supervisor and can shift in response to workers. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; rules/decisions.md)`

### Legitimacy and informal resistance

Official records carry authority even when they conflict with physical evidence. Keel workers distrust this gap and use practical tests: vibration, pressure, visible wear, water movement, condensation, whether a pipe is actually full and whether a repaired machine works. `(rules/vocabulary.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

Resistance includes unauthorized repairs, hidden routes, unregistered tokens, physical keys, local cooperation, falsified routine maintenance, workers standing together, people sharing food, transport and information, and collective refusal to let a single worker be isolated. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

A person can inherit or be assigned household liability. When a Keel resident reaches the relevant age, parental household liability can transfer to them. The draft shows the transfer occurring at age seventeen. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

### Ownership

The world repeatedly distinguishes making something, possessing it, controlling it, receiving value from it, legally owning it and owning equity in it. `(rules/vocabulary.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

A Halyard worker can make a component while a House records ownership of it:

> CONTRIBUTION ACCEPTED / OWNERSHIP: HOUSE / CREATOR BONUS: 14 CREDITS

Standard House employment assigns inventions made with House time, equipment or data to the House. Workers receive wages and a discretionary creator bonus, but no automatic equity or royalties. Attribution can be contested through Charter House review. `(rules/decisions.md)`

### Honest business

**Morrow & Sons** reopens in Keel as a small cooperative shop that builds, services and sells the household purifier to local households at a price above cost but below comparable House industrial units. `(rules/decisions.md)`

The Houses have incentives to control intellectual property, retain exclusive ownership, preserve scale, avoid duplication, protect revenue, prevent independent systems from weakening their position, and own failure rather than share a solution. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

A House may announce or build its own version of a publicly released design more quickly and at wider scale. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

The future retains ordinary physical systems: mining equipment, pumps, pipes, rails, analog gauges, manual regulator wheels, physical keys, paper plans, hand tools, mechanical brackets, workshops, dust, old wiring and damaged infrastructure. `(rules/hard-sf-rules.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

New inventions must be labelled T, EG, S or L when they enter the project. `(rules/hard-sf-rules.md)`

### Control nodes

Control nodes are small, identical white-and-amber devices placed along the shared infrastructure spine and on scanners and system housings. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

They can register shifts, identify workers, process checkpoint status, monitor infrastructure, detect legacy protocols, report activation events and connect physical systems to Alpha's administrative network. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

A node can display or transmit official readings that do not match the physical system. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

### Identity bands and scanners

Workers carry wristbands or identity bands tied to age verification, debt, travel status, assigned work, wage consequences, signal status and location or movement. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

Scanners can display account balances and restrictions publicly enough for nearby workers to see. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

### Drones

Drones are used for surveillance, security patrols, tracking, monitoring access points, protective detention, industrial work and water theft in 2099. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-05-draft.md; input/notes.md)`

Drones use cold-white search beams and can sweep mapped routes after a signal is lost. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

### Water-control technology

The shared water system combines old mine infrastructure, modern pipes, analog gauges, manual regulator wheels, residential lines, industrial uplink lines, data lines carrying official readings and physical control nodes. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

The abandoned lithium works contain newer water-control infrastructure inside obsolete mine systems. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

An official gauge may show a reading such as 62 percent while the corresponding residential pipe is nearly dry and a separate industrial pipe is visibly carrying water. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

### The Measure

The Measure is a compact handheld instrument combining a transparent lens, a balance scale and a water-flow gauge. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

It has three folded arms and can be clamped to a physical pipe and to a data line. Its functions are:

- **SENSE:** show what is actually moving through a physical system;
- **COMPARE:** compare physical movement with Alpha's official reading;
- **TRACE:** follow a discrepancy backward through infrastructure;
- **VERIFY:** seal or authenticate the discovered evidence. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

The Measure depends on a physical connection to the system it reads. It does not automatically decide what should be done with the discrepancy. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

### The Maker's Seal

The Maker's Seal is a palm-sized bronze medallion stamped with an open-hand symbol. It is a maker's mark, not a royal signet. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

Its associated function is to connect ownership to responsibility and recognize actual contribution. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

The Seal can activate when people who genuinely contributed to work are named aloud and the work is not claimed by only one person. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

### The Covenant

The Covenant consists of three linked metal bands, each made from a different metal and engraved with a different name and promise. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

It was designed to link people who honor real obligations and enable communities to make agreements without surrendering everything to one authority. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

The Covenant does not force people to keep an agreement. It depends on people choosing and honoring their obligations. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-06-draft.md)`

Leona's and Adrian's bands link while Mera's remains dark. Mera's band is not required for the new protocol; it remains dark as visible evidence that the old three-custodian model is incomplete. Alex's proposal changes the Covenant's qualifying participants from founders to affected communities. `(rules/decisions.md)`

### Adrian's water system

Adrian's collaborators developed a combined system involving catalytic membrane purification, atmospheric moisture capture, mineral recovery, living biofilter regulation and distributed community water nodes. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

The industrial design combines five pieces developed or held by different people across the Houses. At industrial scale, the pieces use incompatible standards and fail when connected directly. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

A hand-built sleeve can connect incompatible standards. The material gives one simulation an efficiency of 94 percent after this connection. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

A household-scale version uses a folded membrane, alternating power cycles between the biofilter and distributed nodes, a salvaged heat exchanger and heat recovery into the biofilter's power draw. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

The customer-facing specification will state the daily volume, treatment category, service interval and safety warning once those values are set during development. Until then, those values remain unspecified. The purifier does not solve Keel's basin-wide contamination. `(rules/decisions.md)`

Transit connects the three cities through rails and elevated systems. A permission gate lies between Keel and Halyard. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

### Housing and domestic space

Keel housing includes modest apartments with repaired furniture, handmade quilts, old books, faded family photographs, plants in recycled containers, hidden or repurposed storage and domestic rooms connected directly to workshop space. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md)`

Halyard includes rented rooms above maker districts and compact technical workspaces. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

Grandmother requires an urgent 45-credit antibiotic course from a neighborhood clinic. Food is rationed through Keel stations, while lamp fuel is a separate household expense; Alex can delay the fuel but not the medicine. `(rules/decisions.md)`

Tomas fronts Alex the 60 credits needed for the medicine. `(rules/decisions.md)`

The Last Chance casino is part of Keel's history and vocabulary. Its name and old signage remain recognizable. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

## Environment and extraction

Prosperity is a high-desert mining basin. The environment includes exhausted lithium extraction, dust, dry or failing rivers, scarce water, mineral runoff, industrial residue, old mine works, cloud layers above Oasis, controlled gardens and greenhouse terraces, reservoirs and contaminated feeder channels. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

The mining economy has left infrastructure that is both obsolete and still useful. Old mine tunnels can conceal newer water-control systems, routes and physical infrastructure. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

A contaminated feeder channel threatens Keel's water network. Cleaning it may require shutting down half of a Halyard production district. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

The damage is ongoing and only partly reversible: diversion has dried local channels, extraction has left mineral residues and the feeder channel requires industrial remediation. Household purifiers reduce exposure but cannot restore the basin. `(rules/decisions.md)`

Workers in Keel maintain extraction, pumps and aging infrastructure under assignment and surveillance. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

Workers in Halyard create technical components and research, but House employment can separate labor from ownership. A worker may receive a creator bonus while the House owns the component. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

House systems can erase or obscure the names of contributors while retaining their work. The Maker's Seal is designed to oppose that separation by tying creation to attribution and responsibility. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

One collar bears the inscription `WHAT IS NOT MEASURED CAN BE MADE INVISIBLE`. It distinguishes official records from physical reality. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

### The Maker's Seal

A palm-sized bronze medallion with an open-hand symbol. It is worn smooth from being carried and is explicitly a maker's mark rather than a royal signet. It connects ownership to responsibility and recognizes people who actually contributed to work. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md)`

### The Covenant bands

Three linked metal bands, each made from a different metal and engraved with a different name and promise. One band is kept by Leona, one by Adrian and one by Mera. The new structure does not depend on Mera's band activating; its darkness remains a visible sign that the old custodian model is incomplete. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-04-draft.md; rules/decisions.md)`

### Adrian's casino chip

A worn casino chip with a faint looping equation etched into it. Alex has kept it since childhood. It remains connected to Adrian's gambling history and to a technical pattern, but is not a lucky charm. Adrian's gambling caused material harm to his family. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; rules/decisions.md)`

### Adrian's paper plans

Folded, altered paper plans with ink ticks at every third junction and a small pipe symbol beneath one of the ticks. They are physical, hand-marked and usable when Alpha's survey is incomplete or misleading. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

### Identity band

A wrist-worn identity device with a display capable of showing debt, travel status, assignment, wage forfeiture and signal state. Keel workers and residents carry one. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-01-draft.md; input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

### Unregistered travel token

A small physical token with no established material or design. It can pass over a battered platform scanner without producing a normal electronic confirmation. It represents access outside ordinary records. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-02-draft.md)`

### Household purifier

A toolbox-sized unit containing a folded membrane, living biofilter, distributed-node logic, mineral-recovery component, atmospheric-capture component and heat exchanger. Its projected **91 percent efficiency is a simulation, not a guarantee of potable output**. The customer-facing specification will state the daily volume, treatment category, service interval and safety warning once development sets them. The purifier does not solve Keel's basin-wide contamination. Morrow & Sons will build, service and sell it through a cooperative business owned jointly by the five makers. `(input/fifth-draft/chapter-03-draft.md; rules/decisions.md)`

The 91 percent figure is fixed as an efficiency simulation rather than a promise of potable output; no value for the specification has been invented here. `(rules/decisions.md)`

# notes.md

## Verdict

**Needs a pass.** The script’s major causal spine is present, but both cold reads identify repeated failures of reader orientation, especially around TJ, Alpha, the safeguards, the maker ensemble and the Issue 03 governance climax. The execution package also contains a Blocker: the Page 46 layout is an entirely different scene from the approved script, so the book is not ready for production.

## Findings by severity

### Blocker

#### 1. Page 46 layout and thumbnail are the wrong scene

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 02 Page 46; `layouts.md`, Page 46; `thumbnails.md`, Page 46.
- **Observation:** The script ends Issue 02 with Alex separated from Ada, Lina taken behind a service shutter and an Oasis summons. The layout and thumbnail instead depict Leona, Mera and Ada in Leona’s apartment.
- **Problem:** This is a complete scene substitution, not a layout interpretation. It removes the approved cliffhanger and duplicates Issue 03 material.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Layout Agent:** discard the existing Page 46 layout and thumbnail and rebuild the barrier-separation page from the script. **Letterer:** do not letter the apartment dialogue on this page.
- **Role:** layout, letterer.

#### 2. Alpha is essential to the climax but is not introduced clearly enough

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 01 Page 20; Issue 03 Pages 53, 57–60; cold reads’ Issue 03 responses.
- **Observation:** Alpha appears as `LEGACY PROTOCOL DETECTED` on Page 20, but the script never establishes that Alpha is the system governing water, labor, travel, debt and records. Page 57 suddenly asks for a “designated human authority,” and Page 58 offers Alex control over “Debt, travel, water, House review.”
- **Problem:** The central climax depends on a system the reader may understand only as a few glowing nodes. The offer of authority and the rescinding of emergency authority therefore lack dramatic context.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Writer:** plant Alpha’s operational reach before Page 57 through a concrete consequence, not exposition—for example, show the Page 20 trace altering Alex’s travel status or assigning Tomas, and let the display identify Alpha as the authority performing it. At Page 57, make the transfer’s scope visually legible through the existing records rather than adding a speech.
- **Role:** writer.

### Major

#### 3. The Issue 00 hook is disconnected from the principal story

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 00 Pages 8–10; Issue 03 Page 64; `brief.md`, Issue 00 canon.
- **Observation:** The prologue introduces a water theft, a drone component with a white-and-amber node and older Alex’s unexplained wealth. The main story never returns to the thieves, the component, or the question of how Alex became prosperous.
- **Problem:** Both readers report that the opening question is abandoned. The final page leaves the reader with an unrelated travel question, so the book’s first and last narrative promises do not connect.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Director:** decide whether the prologue is intended as a self-contained thematic echo or a plot setup. If self-contained, **Writer:** remove the apparent Alpha-specific node and make the final exchange explicitly about older Alex’s continuing responsibility to protect shared water, without promising an explanation later. If it is a setup, it needs a concrete payoff before Page 64; do not leave the current node as unexplained importance.
- **Role:** director, writer.

#### 4. TJ appears to be introduced twice, and his 2099 identifier is inconsistent

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 00 Pages 1–3 and Page 7; Issue 01 Page 17; `characters.md`, TJ visual lock.
- **Observation:** Issue 00 is written as if TJ is already familiar to older Alex and the granddaughter, but Issue 01 Page 17 presents TJ as a newly discovered folded robot dog. The fixed visual identifier also requires the brass ring in 2099 and plain ceramic lenses in 2043; the prologue does not consistently show the ring.
- **Problem:** The reader cannot confidently tell that the two robots are the same TJ or understand whether Page 17 is his construction, discovery or reactivation.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Writer:** make Page 17 establish that B11 is assembling TJ from the dog chassis, rather than presenting TJ as an unexplained finished object; use one unmistakable visual callback to the 2099 dog. **Character Designer:** show the brass right-eye ring in 2099 and plain scratched ceramic lenses in 2043. Preserve the unexplained transfer of the ring.
- **Role:** writer, character_designer.

#### 5. Page 25’s B11 mistake is not literally intelligible

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 01 Pages 22–25; cold-read reports.
- **Observation:** B11 says, “I predicted we could leave him and remain unseen,” but the script never shows or states that B11 advised leaving Tomas. “Concealment route” and “What would you do?” are not anchored to a visible choice.
- **Problem:** The required B11 fallibility beat becomes opaque instead of emotionally useful.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Writer:** establish B11’s concrete recommendation before the rescue—e.g. a visible route that bypasses Tomas with a stated prediction that the search beam will miss them—then show Alex rejecting it. Keep B11’s admission short after the rescue.
- **Role:** writer.

#### 6. The Page 15 clinic sequence contributes to the Issue 01 pacing drop without sufficiently defining Tomas

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 01 Pages 13–15; cold-read reports.
- **Observation:** Three consecutive pages cover the casino, Ada’s food and the clinic before the hidden workshop. Tomas is introduced as the person fronting medicine, but his role as an older miner and Adrian connection is deferred until Pages 24–26.
- **Problem:** Both readers identify Pages 13–15 as the first likely put-down point. The personal debt is important, but the current sequence feels like cryptic setup rather than a choice under pressure.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Plotter:** compress or combine the casino/food/clinic beats while preserving the 45-credit antibiotic cost and 10-credit terms. **Writer:** identify Tomas through a concrete miner’s action or object at the clinic, and make Alex visibly choose medicine over lamp fuel or travel before accepting the loan.
- **Role:** plotter, writer.

#### 7. The Measure appears without adequate setup

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 01 Pages 27–28; cold-read reports.
- **Observation:** Alex opens “a compact instrument from Adrian’s case” only when the discrepancy must be measured. Its capabilities—physical connection, comparison, tracing and verification—are not previously demonstrated.
- **Problem:** The decisive evidence device feels like a plot token and makes the 62%/18% reveal less earned.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Writer:** plant the Measure in the workshop or B11’s stored equipment on Page 17 or 18, with one visible physical test or limitation. At Page 27, show it clamping separately to pipe and data line before the comparison resolves.
- **Role:** writer.

#### 8. The four Halyard makers remain a fetch-quest sequence

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 02 Pages 37–44; cold reads; `story.md` maker risk.
- **Observation:** Lina, Suri, Jalen and Ren each appear in a short handoff scene, then the purifier is assembled and released within eight pages. The readers report that the makers blur together and their exposure does not yet matter emotionally.
- **Problem:** The story needs the makers to function as people making consequential choices, not as component dispensers. Lina’s Page 46 capture is especially weak because the reader has had little time to invest in her.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Plotter:** collapse redundant retrieval beats and give each remaining maker a distinct choice that changes the build or the risk. **Writer:** make the choice visible: Suri risks the living culture, Jalen chooses to enter the build despite surveillance, Ren commits the repairable connector, and Lina chooses public attribution despite capture risk.
- **Role:** plotter, writer.

#### 9. The Maker’s Seal’s function and the five-maker structure are unclear

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 02 Pages 43–44; Page 63; cold reads.
- **Observation:** Alex names four collaborators on Page 43, then Page 44 lists five contributors without explicitly naming Alex. The Seal appears for the first time on Page 44 and seems to block an exclusive claim, but the relation between attribution, House ownership and public release is not shown.
- **Problem:** The reader cannot tell whether the Seal transfers ownership, blocks a corporation, verifies contribution or simply makes the design free. The five-way Morrow & Sons ownership is then asserted only on Page 63.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Writer:** name all five makers—including Alex—in the public record and show the Seal verifying contribution rather than transferring property. **Plotter:** plant the cooperative business as the intended destination of the design before the release, even if the shop opens later. **Letterer:** keep the five names legible without turning the panel into an exposition screen.
- **Role:** plotter, writer, letterer.

#### 10. The Page 46 danger does not pay off in Issue 03

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 02 Page 46; Issue 03 Pages 47–49; cold reads.
- **Observation:** Lina is taken behind a service shutter, but Issue 03 begins with Alex and Ada traveling separately and then proceeds to Ada/Leona. Lina is not shown being released, protected or participating again until her name appears on the Page 63 shop sign.
- **Problem:** The cliffhanger promises immediate danger to Ada and Lina, but the script silently resolves Lina’s situation off-panel.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Writer:** show a minimal consequence and status for Lina before the group reaches the civic hall—such as a public review notice, a release under the new process or Lina appearing at the hearing. Do not make the rescue a second climax; close the open danger visibly.
- **Role:** writer.

#### 11. Leona and Mera are insufficiently differentiated in the script

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 03 Pages 49–60; cold reads.
- **Observation:** Both women are older Oasis officials speaking in controlled administrative language about past failures and public accountability. Mera enters without a clear action establishing her authority or relationship to Alpha.
- **Problem:** Readers confuse the two women and do not know whether Mera is ally, antagonist, former executive or witness until very late.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Writer:** give Mera one early, unmistakable institutional action—such as authorizing the Page 20 trace or appearing on the enforcement record—and one concrete cost on Page 53. Give Leona the distinct action of choosing public exposure to Ada’s challenge. Preserve both women’s accountability without adding biography.
- **Role:** writer.

#### 12. The Covenant activation remains visually and causally under-explained

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 01 Page 17; Issue 03 Pages 52, 56 and 60.
- **Observation:** Adrian’s band appears on Page 17; Leona’s band links to it on Page 52; Page 56 displays three safeguards; Page 60 registers the revised protocol, but the separate status of Mera’s dark band and the change from founder custodians to affected communities are not visually carried through.
- **Problem:** The reader sees an apparently magical band response without understanding what obligation was performed, what remains incomplete and why the new process is not simply restoration of the old Covenant.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Writer/Layout Agent:** at registration, show Leona and Adrian’s bands linked, Mera’s band dark and separate, and the representatives—not the founders—taking the next procedural position. Keep the Covenant physical and bounded; no new explanatory lecture.
- **Role:** writer, layout.

#### 13. The distributed protocol reads as a civics diagram rather than a process under pressure

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 03 Pages 60–62; cold reads.
- **Observation:** Page 60 proposes three representatives from each locality; Page 61 presents three tables; Page 62 catches the House category error. The script does not show how the representatives were selected, whose mandate Tomas carries or what happens when they challenge the proposal.
- **Problem:** The ending’s proof of change lacks the immediate procedural stakes that would make the caught manipulation dramatic.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Writer:** show one concrete mandate per locality—paper strip, open-meeting record or residents instructing representatives—and make the decision hinge on whether the representatives can approve or reject the sheet. Keep the representative ensemble visually simple and name only the people needed for action.
- **Role:** writer.

#### 14. The 420-unit manipulation is not fully legible

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 03 Page 62.
- **Observation:** House purifier crates are labeled `HOUSE INVENTORY — NOT CONNECTED`, while the allocation sheet lists them as community supply.
- **Problem:** The physical image proves they are not connected now, but it does not clearly show that the House is counting owned inventory as already delivered supply or that the proposal would approve this classification.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Writer:** make the same public record contain both the category `COMMUNITY SUPPLY` and the House-owned inventory identifier. **Layout Agent:** stage the sheet, crates and gauge in a clear visual sequence so the discrepancy is read before Tomas rejects it.
- **Role:** writer, layout.

#### 15. The ending’s debt reduction and Morrow & Sons operation are asserted, not earned

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 03 Page 63; `facts.md`, economics; cold reads.
- **Observation:** The script jumps to “MONTHS LATER,” shows a shop, a paid medicine advance and Alex’s debt reduced from 418,607 to 402,110 credits. It does not show the work or payments producing that reduction.
- **Problem:** The required continuing debt and visible repayment are present as labels rather than consequences. The reader reasonably experiences the final balance as “not much changed” rather than as costly progress.
- **Smallest repair direction:** **Plotter:** use Page 63’s existing four panels to show the shop’s work ledger, Alex’s wage/payment and Tomas’s completed terms as parts of an ongoing accounting chain. **Writer:** explicitly distinguish the medicine debt being paid from the larger administrative debt, and show the final balance as the result of visible payments rather than protocol relief.
- **Role:** plotter, writer.

#### 16. The final page’s question about Ada is too abstract

- **Location:** `script.md`, Issue 03 Page 64; cold reads.

Give Ada a final action—folding one form, leaving both open, or stepping toward the gate—that preserves uncertainty while making the question personal.

## Plausibility ledger

- **64-page structure — HOLDS:** The script contains Pages 1–64 with the required 10-page prologue and three 18-page issues.
- **Issue 00 chronology — HOLDS WITH RISK:** The prologue is set in 2099 and does not explain the safeguards or debt. The unexplained white-and-amber drone node risks creating an unauthorized Alpha connection.
- **Issue 00 hook — UNDER-SUPPORTED:** The prologue raises the thieves’ motive and older Alex’s prosperity but the principal story never answers or deliberately reframes either question.
- **TJ visual continuity — CONTRADICTED:** 2099 requires the brass right-eye ring; the script does not consistently deliver it. 2043 requires plain scratched ceramic lenses.
- **Tomas loan — CONFLICTED:** Script and brief use 45 credits; facts/world retain 60. Normalize before production.
- **House names — CONFLICTED:** Brief/script use Caldera, Vector and Orbital; facts/world retain Veyr, Cairn and Ravel. Normalize before production.
- **Alpha’s scope — UNDER-SUPPORTED:** The ending depends on Alpha’s emergency authority, but the script never concretely establishes its governing reach before the transfer offer.
- **Measure — UNDER-SUPPORTED:** The tool’s appearance and operation are plausible within the hard-SF baseline, but it is introduced too late and its physical limitations are not planted.
- **Maker’s Seal — PARTIALLY HOLDS:** It can verify named contribution and block a single exclusive claim, but the script risks implying that it itself changes property law or makes the design public.
- **Purifier — HOLDS WITH LIMITATION:** The 91% figure is correctly labeled an efficiency simulation and not potable output. No unresolved customer specification should be invented.
- **Covenant — PARTIALLY HOLDS:** Leona states an obligation, accepts a consequence and performs the public action before activation. The band continuity and physical mechanism remain under-supported.
- **Distributed protocol — UNDER-SUPPORTED:** The script registers the protocol and stages the first review, but selection, mandate, recall and representatives’ authority are not shown sufficiently.
- **First review — UNDER-SUPPORTED:** The House inventory discrepancy is visible but needs a clearer record connecting owned units to the false “community supply” figure.
- **Debt reduction — UNDER-SUPPORTED:** The final 402,110-credit balance is canonically required but the script does not show the visible work and payments producing it.
- **Morrow & Sons — UNDER-SUPPORTED:** The shop appears only as an ending status image. Joint ownership, wages, equal profit shares and customer-serving operation need a concrete visual bridge.
- **Adrian’s fate — HOLDS:** The station record supports presumed death and legal missing status without recovering a body.
- **Alex’s mother — HOLDS:** No prohibited information is added. Preserve the standing rule that she left Adrian after he lost everything and nothing else is learned.
- **Page 46 execution — CONTRADICTED:** The layout and thumbnail depict the wrong scene. This is an execution Blocker.
- **Hard-SF baseline — GENERALLY HOLDS:** Pipes, gauges, physical keys, data shards and manual repairs support the setting. The Covenant must remain staged as a bounded physical safeguard rather than unexplained magic.

# First Read: Prosperity, Issue 00, pages 1–3 (Auditions A and B)

I read these as the assigned reader: 16, it's homework, it's the night before, and I want it to be bad. **I read A first.** So B was never fully cold for me. By B I already knew the dog comes apart and there are water thieves on a barge, and the surprise of the dog falling to pieces had been used up.

I only had the art as described, the captions, the balloons and the sound effects. A few lines in the art descriptions read like notes to the artist ("seventy years after the main story," "a broken constellation," "not a wave, not yet an alarm"). I ignored those, because a reader would only see the picture.

---

## VERSION A

### Pulled me forward
- **Issue 00, page 1, panel 4.** The dog steps off the dock and falls apart in mid-air. "KLAK." It's the first thing that made me stop rolling my eyes. I didn't expect it, it isn't explained, and I wanted to know if it was broken or meant to do that. That's good confusion.
- **Page 2, panels 2–3.** The head floating on its own with the light catching the eye ring, and the legs swimming separately underwater. It's creepy and cool. The dog is hunting something, and nobody has told me so. I worked it out, and I liked working it out.
- **Page 3, panel 3.** "Nobody gets water this clean. Not fairly." / "Then he stole it first. Keep pulling." That's the best line in either version. Suddenly the thieves aren't just villains, and the old man maybe isn't the good guy. I sat up a little.
- **Page 3, panel 4.** The head clicking onto the hull under the thieves, watching. Quiet, and a bit scary.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 2, panel 4.** The hoses swelling. I already knew they were taking water from panel 1, so I skimmed it.
- **Page 1, panels 1–2.** A dark lake, then an old man standing still. Standard opening shot. I gave it a second and moved on.

### I was confused
- **Who is the old man?** He stands still on page 1, panel 2 and then he's gone. He never speaks and nobody says his name. "He owns the lake" is all I get. I don't know if he sent the dog, if he's even awake, or if he cares.
- **Why is water stolen with drones and a tanker?** I get from the dialogue that clean water is rare and valuable, but nothing tells me why. Is the world out of water? Is this normal? Confused but still interested. It isn't a leak yet, but it will be if page 4 doesn't say something.
- **Is the dog his?** I assumed so, because it leaves his dock. Nothing confirms it.
- The "terraces" around the lake. In the art this is just a lake with steps around it. I would never guess it used to be a mine pit, so if that matters, I missed it.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First appears | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Lake Keel | Page 1, panel 1 caption | No. It's a name on a lake. |
| 2099 / why the date matters | Page 1, panel 1 | No. I know it's the future, nothing else. |
| The old man's name (Alex) | Never said | No. I only know him as "he." |
| The dog's name (TJ) | Never said | No. To me he's "the robot dog." |
| What the dog is for | Page 1, panel 3 | Partly. I figure he's a guard. |
| Why clean water is valuable / stolen | Page 2, panel 4; page 3, panel 3 | Partly. "Nobody gets water this clean." No why. |
| What "stole it first" refers to | Page 3, panel 3 | No. It's a hook, not an answer. |

### Lines I read twice
- "Doesn't have to. He owns the lake." Once was enough, and it worked.
- "Then he stole it first." I read it twice, but because I liked it, not because I was lost. It took a second to realise it's an accusation against the old man.
- I didn't give up on any lines. There are only six balloons, so there isn't much to trip on.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Old man: yes, he's the only old guy. But he's a shape, not a person.
- The dog: easy, with the rust and the brass ring on one eye. The most memorable character on the page.
- Thief 1 and Thief 2: I can't tell them apart at all. Same gear, same job. Thief 1 is maybe the one with doubts ("Not fairly")? I'd forget that by page 5.

### I felt something
- A small chill at page 3, panel 4, when the head watches them from the dark.
- A flicker of "wait, who's the bad guy here" at "Then he stole it first."
- Nothing for the old man. He's too far away to feel anything about.

### I predicted
- The dog puts itself back together on the barge and wrecks the operation, or scares them off.
- The old man turns out to have done something shady to get the lake, and the book is about how.
- I don't think the thieves are going to be okay.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A rich old man who controls the last clean water in a dried-out future, and whether he got it honestly.

### Where I would have put it down
Probably not in these three pages. They're short and the dog carries them. But if page 4 is more silent old man, that's where I'd go back to my phone. The person the book seems to be about hasn't done or said anything yet.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
I'd turn the page, but I wouldn't rush. The head on the hull is a nice creepy beat, but it isn't really a cliffhanger. Nobody I care about is in danger. The dog is cool, but I don't know if it can get hurt, and the thieves are strangers. What actually pulls me forward is the question from panel 3: what did he steal? That's a real question, but it's about a man I've barely seen.

## VERSION B

*(Second read. The dog falling apart did nothing to me this time, because I'd seen it in A.)*

### Pulled me forward
- **Issue 00, page 1, panel 2.** "Is that supposed to happen?" / "Not usually." That made me almost laugh, and it's the moment I started to like the old man. He's dry. The kid is asking what I'm asking, so I have someone to stand next to.
- **Page 1, panel 4.** "Should we call someone?" / "Let's see what they came to take." Now I know he's calm, he's watching, and he's maybe a bit dangerous. It's a person making a choice, not a statue.
- **Page 3, panel 1.** "The old man with the lake?" / "The old man with everything." Good. It tells me he's rich and that people talk about him, and it makes him sound bigger than he looks on the shore.
- **Page 3, panel 4.** The drone's intake shutters closing around the dog's head. I honestly didn't know if the dog was attacking or getting eaten. I leaned in.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 2, panel 1.** Head on a float, torso and two legs moving separately, and a fourth leg holding onto a rail. I lost track of where all the parts were and skimmed. Too many pieces to follow.
- **Page 2, panel 3** and **page 3, panel 3.** Head tilts, head bumps a ripple, head reaches the drone. It's a lot of small head moments. I started flicking past the sound effects (TIK, VMMMMM, KLIK).
- **Page 3, panel 2.** The binocular view. It shows me what I already saw on page 2, panel 4.

### I was confused
- **Page 1, panel 1.** The dog is already out on the lake coming apart in the very first picture. I never saw it leave the shore, so I wasn't sure where it came from or whose it was until the old man reacts.
- **Page 2, panel 1.** "A small magnetic float hidden beneath its jaw." If it's hidden, I can't see it, so to me the head is just floating somehow. Also, why is one leg on a rail? Confused and a bit detached, because I couldn't build the picture.
- **Page 2, panel 4.** He raises a hand. Is he waving at the thieves? Signalling the dog? Surrendering? I only see a hand.
- **Is the dog going after the drone or the barge?** In A it went for the barge. Here it's the drone, and I'm not sure what grabbing a drone does.
- Why the water is worth stealing. Same gap as A, even slightly less explained.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First appears | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Lake Keel / 2099 | Assumed from the issue title. B's page 1 has no caption described, so it's unclear I even see it. | No. |
| Phantum | Page 3, panel 1 ("That's Phantum's place.") | Partly. It's the old man's surname. I never get a first name. |
| The old man's first name (Alex) | Never said | No. |
| The dog's name (TJ) | Never said | No. Still "the robot dog." |
| The granddaughter | Page 1, panel 1 | Partly. A kid, probably his. Nobody says so or names her. |
| Why water is stolen / valuable | Page 2, panel 2 ("It's a lake, not a vault.") | No. |
| "Water paid for it? / Or water made him rich." | Page 3, panel 2 | No. I don't know what "it" is. |

### Lines I read twice
- **"Then they know we're polite."** (page 2, panel 4). I read it twice and still only half get it. Is it a joke? A threat? Does he mean they're being polite by not calling the police? It sounds clever, but I couldn't work out what it means.
- **"Water paid for it?" / "Or water made him rich."** (page 3, panel 2). I read it twice and these sound like the same thing to me. Paid for what? I gave up on it.
- **"It's a lake, not a vault."** One extra beat to get it: they think nobody's guarding it. Fine after that.
- "Let's see what they came to take." Once was fine, but it's a bit movie-ish.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Old man (Phantum): yes, clearly. He has a voice, a little humour and a mood.
- Granddaughter: yes. She's the scared, normal one, but she has no name and no personality beyond asking questions.
- The dog: yes, but less distinct than in A. Two scratched lenses instead of the brass ring, so nothing to remember him by.
- Thief 1 and Thief 2: a little better than A. Thief 2 is the one who knows who Phantum is and sounds bitter. Thief 1 asks the questions. Still only barely.

### I felt something
- A small warm thing at page 1, panel 4, when the kid reaches for his sleeve and he doesn't look away from the dog. It tells me something about him, that the dog matters more to him right now.
- A bit of worry for the dog at page 3, panel 4, because the shutters close and it might be trapped.
- Less creepiness than A. With people talking on the shore, it feels less like a horror scene and more like a story.

### I predicted
- The dog sabotages the drone, the drone crashes, and the thieves panic.
- The granddaughter is going to learn something bad about her grandfather and how he got the lake. She's set up to be the one who asks.
- Phantum is not a simple good guy.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
An old man whose family thinks of him one way, and the rest of the world sees as the man who got rich off the last clean water.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 2. With the leg on the rail, the hidden float, the head bumping a ripple and "Then they know we're polite," that's the page where I felt the book showing off and I wasn't following. I'd have kept going because of page 1, but page 2 is the dip.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
More than A, but not desperately. The shutters closing on the dog is closer to a real cliffhanger, because I don't know if he wins or gets chewed up, and I've just watched the old man care about him. But the dog isn't someone I know yet. It's a loud click on a machine. I'd turn the page to see the drone, not because I'm attached.

---

## Which one I would keep reading, and the moment that decided it

**B, just barely.** It was decided at **B, page 1, panel 2: "Is that supposed to happen?" / "Not usually."** In A I spent three pages with a silent old man and two thieves I couldn't tell apart, so the only character I had was a robot. In B there's a person, a kid asking my questions, and an old guy with a sense of humour, so I had someone to follow.

That said, A had the line I'll actually remember ("Then he stole it first") and the creepier, clearer dog. B lost me on page 2 in a way A never did, and two of B's lines ("Then they know we're polite," "Water paid for it? / Or water made him rich") went over my head. Neither version told me why water is worth stealing, and both are going to need to soon.

## One-sentence aftertaste of each

- **A:** A creepy, silent robot dog and one great accusation, but the old man is a shadow I couldn't care about.
- **B:** An old man and his granddaughter I'd actually follow, buried under a busy page 2 and a couple of lines that sounded clever and meant nothing to me.

# Cold Read: Prosperity

I read it from start to finish in one sitting, pages only, as homework the night before it's due. I went in wanting it to be bad. Everything below is what happened to me, in order.

---

## Issue 00: Lake Keel, 2099 (pages 1–10)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 1, panel 1.** A robot dog that comes apart mid-step and keeps walking in pieces is a good first image. I didn't go back to my phone on page 1, and this panel is why.
- **Page 2, panel 1.** The head floats across the lake while the legs go along a rail. It's weird and specific, not generic sci-fi. I wanted to see what it would do.
- **Page 7.** The lost leg sits on the bottom, its magnet pulses, then it snaps back onto the head and drags it home. Best page of the issue. Nobody explains it and nobody needed to.
- **Page 8, panel 2.** "You could have stopped them." / "I could have started something." The old man let it happen on purpose, and that made me curious about him.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Pages 4–6.** The drone fight. I followed it, but it's all clamping, buckling and spraying, and I was skimming SFX by page 5.

### I was confused
- **Page 1, panel 1.** "His right eye carries a small adjustable brass ring." Whose eye? Alex's or TJ's? On page 3 it's TJ's eye-ring. On page 18 B11 has the brass ring. By the end of the book I still couldn't tell you if TJ and B11 share a part, or if I misread page 1.
- **Page 4, panel 3.** The granddaughter calls him "Alex", not grandpa. I stopped to work out whether she's really his granddaughter.
- **Page 5, panel 2.** "It has the route." What route? Route to where?
- **Page 9, panel 4.** "No white-and-amber control node." I'm being told something is missing that I've never seen. It meant nothing to me.
- **Page 10.** "That isn't why they came here." / "No. It isn't." OK, so why? I'm confused but curious. This is the hook, and it mostly works. But see the end of the book.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First seen | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Alex Phantum (as a name I'd know) | p1 | Yes, issue 01 |
| TJ | p1 | Sort of: Adrian's robot dog, p17 |
| Siphon drones / "the route" | p2, p5 | No |
| Why water is worth stealing in 2099 | p2–3 | Partly (issue 01 water shortage) |
| "The old man with everything": why he's rich | p3 | **No. Never.** |
| Adrian (the casino chip) | p9 | Dad, issue 01. Never really known as a person |
| White-and-amber control node | p9 | Shows up p19, still not explained |
| Lake terraces / old mine rails | p7–8 | Barely |

### Lines I read twice
- p3: "Water paid for it?" / "Or water made him rich."
- p6: "He always sees the part that costs." I gave up on this one.

Alex, the girl and TJ are clear. Thief 1 and Thief 2 are interchangeable, and that's fine.

A small thing on page 8, panel 4, when the girl kneels for the broken dog. Nothing bigger.

### I predicted
The drone part would turn out to be evidence that someone (not random thieves) was after Alex. I also predicted the book would come back to this night at the end.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
An old rich man who owns a lake lets water thieves go because something bigger is behind them, and he's hiding a past.

### Where I would have put it down
Nowhere. It's short and visual and I got through it.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Mild yes. "No. It isn't." is a real question, but it's about a man I've known for ten pages. I'd turn the page tonight because it's short. I wasn't hooked.

# analysis.md (from the room)

# Analysis: *Prosperity*, pages 1–64

Read cold, pages only. Page parity is from the script: odd pages are on the right, even pages on the left, so a reveal lands best on an even page, just after the reader turns.

---

## The political read

| Reading | Signal | Pages that carry it |
|---|---|---|
| **Progressive** | **Strong on the surface** | p12: debt is passed to a 17-year-old by a "PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER". p14: residents queue at a dry ration channel while Halyard's lights glow above. p28: "REPORTED 62% / DELIVERED 18%", and Ada asks "Who gets the rest?" Alex: "Someone with a full pipe." p34: "OWNERSHIP: CALDERA HOUSE / CREATOR: UNLISTED / CREATOR BONUS: 14 CREDITS". The words "affected people" and "community supply" (pp51–52, 61–63). |
| **Socialist** | **Some** | p29: workers "close ranks" against the foreman. That reads as a walkout. p63: the ledger has "EQUAL PROFIT SHARES". p62, Tomas: "Owned units aren't delivered water." On its own that line can read as being against owning things. |
| **Capitalist in a bad way** | **Some, and it is ambiguous** | The Houses (Caldera, Vector, Orbital), "Director" Lock, clerks who drag Lina through a shutter (p46), and "AREA CONSOLIDATION — EFFICIENCY REVIEW" (p38). The pages never say whether a House is a company, a guild or a chartered arm of the state. A 16-year-old will default to "megacorp". |
| **Libertarian** | **Strong in the story** | Alex refuses the debt-clearing assignment (p35–36). He refuses the executive lever ("No executive designation," p59). Central authority is withdrawn: "EMERGENCY AUTHORITY: RESCINDED" (p60). Property is left alone: "EXISTING ALLOCATIONS, OWNERSHIP RECORDS AND AGREEMENTS: UNCHANGED PENDING HUMAN PROCESS" (p60). Verification is spread out instead of trusted to one authority (pp28, 60–62). Alpha, a faceless central system, is the real antagonist (pp20, 57). |
| **Conservative** | **Some** | Alex keeps his word to Tomas (pp15, 23, 63), cares for his grandmother, and pays down the debt himself instead of escaping it (p63: 418,607 falls to 402,110). Leona taking on a public obligation (p52). |
| **Capitalist in a good way** | **Strong at the end, weak before it** | A customer buys repairable equipment. Ren on p40: "build it so a customer can repair it." The honest warning label on p42 ("NOT A POTABLE-OUTPUT GUARANTEE"). The small shop on p63 with a real ledger: customer payment, materials, maintenance, wages. The informal loan, with the terms written down (p15) and paid in full (p63). |

**Surface versus story.** Issues 01 and 02 open like a dystopia about debt and the company town: a corporate-looking system takes the water and takes the inventor's credit. That invites the progressive reading. The story under it argues for something else. The villains are a central planner (Alpha) and privileged charter-holders. The hero refuses every handout and every crown. Property records stay intact. The ending is a customer-serving shop and a loan repaid.

**Who stops reading because of the surface.** A conservative-leaning teacher or parent flipping through Issue 01 sees debt bondage, a foreman in a harness and workers closing ranks on p29, and may shelve the book before Issue 03. A student who reads only Issues 00–01 for the assignment comes away with "the system is rigged." The rescue of that reading comes from p35 on.

**Does the book conclude, or leave a reader concluding, that free enterprise is bad?** **No.** Pp35–36 and 59 refuse the bailout and the central control. P60 leaves ownership records unchanged. P63 makes an honest business the resolution. The residual risks are pp34, 44 and 62, covered below.

---

## What might offend, and whom

| Issue | Who is offended | Likelihood | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| A 17-year-old inherits a parent's debt by automatic transfer, with no hint anywhere that this is wrong or unusual | A financial educator at a real bank, who knows debts do not pass to children this way and fears students will absorb it as fact | Medium | p12 |
| The Houses read as "big business" villains: a creator's bonus of 14 credits, an exclusive claim, consolidation, clerks forcing a worker through a shutter | YAC staff and Reynolds, if students read the Houses as ordinary companies | Medium | pp34, 38, 46 |
| Labor-solidarity image: miners closing ranks against the foreman | A conservative parent or school board member | Low–medium | p29 |
| Left-coded civic vocabulary: "affected people," "community supply," "temporary representatives," "recall" | A conservative teacher, and YAC because it must stay nonpartisan in every district | Medium | pp51–52, 60–61, 63 |
| Gambling: the father's casino chip is the magic key that opens the hidden workshop, under a "LAST CHANCE" casino sign | YAC ("gambling made glamorous for minors"). The book does frame Adrian's gambling as a flaw: "One of them paid better... Not ours" (p13), "He was still a gambler" (p55). | Low | pp13, 16–17 |
| Gender: the women are skilled (Lina, Suri and Ren each bring a component), but the man assembles and names; Ada's climactic act is catching the hero's wrist as his conscience (pp58–59); the one mother abandoned her child (p50); Grandmother and granddaughter are never named; the shop shared with three women is "Morrow & Sons" (p63) | A woman reader of 16 or older would notice the unnamed women and the "& Sons" sign. "An old man wrote it" is a plausible reaction, though not a certain one. Ada does lead physically (p32 "Don't trust the rail"; p45), and she gets her own Issue 03 thread. | Medium | pp1–10, 15–16, 50, 58–59, 63 |
| Age gaps between characters | Nothing. There is no romance. Tomas is an adult lending to a minor, but the terms are written down and fair. | Low | p15 |
| Real names | Nothing. No real person is named. "B11" is never linked to anyone real. | None | — |
| Addiction | Only Adrian's gambling, as above. No substances. | Low | p13 |
| Illness | Grandmother needs antibiotics (p15). It is handled plainly and drives the loan. | None | p15 |
| Race | No race is described. The names suggest a mix (Okafor, Anik, Orr). The risk sits in the art: if poor Keel is drawn darker-skinned and glass Halyard white, the vertical class geography (mine → glass towers → above the clouds) becomes a racial one. | Low, depends on art | pp14, 33, 48 |
| Setting | Mining-town Keel with old mine rails reads as Colorado. A Colorado audience will enjoy that, and no one will be offended by it. | None | pp7, 11 |
| Death | Adrian drowning on an archive recording. It is restrained. | None | p54 |
